docs.title: Decision Answers
docs.text: For the integration flow, read Decision Model-Related Protocols. For question IDs, options, and rubric definitions, use Decision Questions.

docs.title: Response fields
docs.text:
DecisionResponse.answers maps the request's question IDs to DecisionAnswer values. Each answer separates its value from optional provider confidence.

Protocol field and type Meaning System One OpenAI Decisions DecisionResponse.id: Option<String> Provider response identifier, when available. Optional id The current adapter reads no response ID and returns none DecisionResponse.model: Option<ModelId> Provider-reported model identifier. Optional model model DecisionResponse.answers: BTreeMap<String, DecisionAnswer> Answers matched by question ID. answers object answers[], identified by name DecisionAnswer.value: DecisionValue Typed estimate matching the question's kind. noul, choice, or score probability, choice, or score DecisionAnswer.provider_confidence: Option<ProviderConfidence> Provider-specific confidence with its own scale and meaning. Optional confidence Optional confidence DecisionResponse.usage: Usage Available token counts; absent counts remain unknown. Deserialized into Usage Counts normalized into Usage, separating cache reads and writes from aggregate input

docs.title: Answer values
docs.text:
Variant and fields Contract System One OpenAI Decisions BooleanEstimate::Value(bool) A Boolean-only judgment with no implied certainty. The supplied adapter returns a probability instead The supplied adapter returns a probability instead BooleanEstimate::ProbabilityTrue(Probability) Probability of true on a [0, 1] scale. The algorithm chooses any threshold. type: "noul", field noul type: "predicate", field probability DecisionValue::Choice with selected: String and probabilities: Option<BTreeMap<String, Probability>> Select a declared ID. When supplied, the distribution covers every declared option. choice; optional ID-keyed probabilities choice; probabilities[] with option value and probability, converted to a map DecisionValue::Score with value: ScoreValue and probabilities: Option<Vec<Probability>> Position in 0..=N-1; the optional distribution follows the question's level order. score; optional probabilities keyed by numeric strings, reordered by level score; numeric value / probability entries, reordered by level

DecisionValue::Boolean wraps a BooleanEstimate. An absent distribution stays unknown; it does not become a one-hot distribution. Likewise, a Boolean-only answer does not imply probability zero or one.

Probability, ScoreValue, and ProviderConfidence are public numeric wrappers. Their stated ranges and meanings are contracts, not validation performed by their constructors. Keep answer probability separate from provider confidence.

docs.title: Matching and errors
docs.text:
Retain the request when converting a response. Question IDs identify the expected kind; choice IDs identify valid selections; rubric order gives scores meaning. Both clients match responses against the request and perform format-specific checks. An unexpected ID, kind, or malformed supported response can produce LlmClientError::ResponseTranslation.

The OpenAI adapter treats a refusal as an error because DecisionValue has no refusal variant. Transport failures and upstream HTTP errors also surface through LlmClientError. A host converts its work result to libsy::Result<DecisionResponse> when replying through CallDecision::respond.

These clients do not retry automatically. Their constructors accept a timeout covering the HTTP request and reading the body. See the question reference's adapter links for the exact conversion and error paths.

docs.title: Conversion guarantees
docs.text:
Supported decision fields map directly while retaining question IDs, answer probabilities, rubric positions, and confidence. OpenAI text-only fields carry structured protocol values as JSON text. This preserves content, rather than making the wire formats identical or guaranteeing arbitrary JSON round trips.

The provider must actually report a field for it to be available. Keep missing IDs, confidence, distributions, and usage unknown. For cache and reasoning token semantics, see LLM usage.

Return to the decision protocol guide to connect the response to your application's execution loop.

docs.title: Decision Questions
docs.text:
For the integration flow and a request example, read Decision Model-Related Protocols. For result interpretation and provider response mappings, continue to Decision Answers.

System One is a common API for open decision models, including Jev. SystemOneClient uses /v1/systemone; OpenAiDecisionClient uses /v1/decisions. Both accept DecisionRequest.

docs.title: Request fields
docs.text:
Protocol field and type Meaning System One OpenAI Decisions DecisionRequest.model: Option<ModelId> Selected decision model. The HTTP adapters require it before sending. model model DecisionRequest.context: Value Shared conversation, application state, or other material to evaluate. JSON-valued state Text-valued input; structured values are serialized as JSON text DecisionRequest.questions: BTreeMap<String, DecisionQuestion> Independent questions keyed by stable IDs. questions object, keyed by ID questions[], with each ID in name DecisionQuestion.instructions: Value Instructions for one question. JSON-valued instructions Text-valued instructions; structured values become JSON text DecisionQuestion.kind: DecisionKind Expected Boolean, choice, or rubric-score answer. Question type and criteria Question type, with choices or levels where applicable

Question IDs identify the answers. Preserve them through conversion; an array position alone is not a replacement for an ID. Context is shared across the request, while each question has its own instructions.

docs.title: Question kinds
docs.text:
Kind and fields Contract System One OpenAI Decisions DecisionKind::Boolean with true_description: Option<Value> and false_description: Option<Value> Ask for a Boolean judgment or probability of true. Descriptions define the two answers when needed. type: "noul"; descriptions in criteria.true and criteria.false type: "predicate"; descriptions are included in instruction text because there are no separate fields DecisionKind::Choice with options: Vec<ChoiceOption> Declare a nonempty list of options with unique IDs, preserving their order in the protocol. type: "choice"; criteria maps option IDs to descriptions type: "choice"; choices[] carries value and optional description DecisionKind::Score with levels: Vec<Value> Declare at least two levels, ordered low to high and indexed from zero. type: "score"; criteria is the level array type: "score"; levels[].label carries each level's text ChoiceOption.id: String Stable ID used by the selected answer and any distribution. Key in criteria choices[].value ChoiceOption.description: Option<Value> Optional meaning when the ID alone is insufficient. JSON-valued description; absent description becomes null Text description when supplied; structured values become JSON text

Choice questions can contain more than two options. A score is a position on the declared rubric, including fractional positions; it is not an arbitrary numeric measurement. Keep the question's levels when interpreting the answer.

docs.title: Construction and validation
docs.text:
The fields are public. Constructing or deserializing a DecisionRequest does not enforce all question contracts. Supply a selected model for HTTP calls, valid option IDs, and a correctly ordered rubric. The adapters apply their format-specific checks; they are not a general validation layer for every possible backend.

Enums in the protocol's own serialized form use snake-case type tags with a data payload. Provider payloads use the mappings above. Serializing the protocol value directly is therefore not a substitute for a provider adapter.

docs.title: Provider adapters
docs.text:
The System One implementation and OpenAI Decisions implementation are reference examples of request encoding and response conversion. Both supplied clients make one attempt per call, with a timeout covering the request and reading the body.

You can use either supplied client, or convert an existing client's data yourself. RoutedDecisionClient is an optional shared client interface. The guide's direct call handling shows the application boundary; Decision Answers covers the response contract.

docs.title: LLM Requests
docs.text: This reference covers request fields and the built-in provider mappings. For the integration flow and a construction example, read LLM-Related Protocols. For the reply, continue to Responses and Streams.

docs.title: Request envelope
docs.text:
An algorithm receives Request. Its llm_request contains the conversation; the remaining envelope data belongs to the application.

Field and type Meaning Request.llm_request: LlmRequest The conversation and settings used by the algorithm and model client. Request.metadata: Option<Metadata> Optional session, correlation, and routing metadata. Request.raw_request: Option<Value> An optional original body retained by the host. Translation codecs do not read this field.

Codec replay uses LlmRequest.preservation, separately from the envelope's raw body. See preservation and edits before changing a decoded request.

docs.title: Conversation fields
docs.text:
These mappings describe the built-in codecs. Supported features also depend on the destination model. Select a Rust field or type for its full crate definition.

docs.title: Messages and tool content
docs.text:
Message.role is a Role; Message.content is an ordered Vec<ContentBlock>. The content variants cover text, reasoning, media, tools, MCP activity, refusals, and unknown provider blocks. An unknown block retains its source format and raw JSON. Its retention does not make it usable in a different API.

docs.title: Stream lifetime and preservation
docs.text:
Pass original LlmResponseStreamEvent values through when exact same-format parsed-JSON replay matters. replace_normalized() returns an event with the new chunks and clears its stale raw replay data.

LlmResponse::into_agg().await consumes the stream and folds its normalized chunks into an AggLlmResponse. Stream item failures, decode failures, and in-band upstream errors become errors. Aggregation does not preserve the original provider event sequence, MCP activity, unknown blocks, or all response extensions. The current accumulator also folds output indices into one assistant output.

Dropping a stream stops local consumption. It cannot guarantee that the provider stops generation or billing. See concurrency and cancellation for host-owned work, and Translation for decoding, encoding, and finishing provider streams.

docs.title: LLM Translation
docs.text:
For a small integration example, read Use the translation crate. For field mappings, use LLM Requests and Responses and Streams.

TranslationEngine converts between provider JSON and Switchyard protocol types. It makes no network calls. WireFormat identifies the built-in Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages formats. FormatId can also identify custom formats registered through the codec interfaces.

docs.title: Engine operations
docs.text:
All operations below are methods of TranslationEngine. The request and buffered-response methods take a TranslationPolicy.

Method Input and result Use it for decode_request Provider JSON to LlmRequest, plus diagnostics. Accepting a request from a provider-facing gateway or harness. encode_request LlmRequest to provider JSON, plus diagnostics. Sending a call through an existing client. translate_request Source provider JSON to target provider JSON. Direct request conversion without handling the protocol value yourself. decode_response Provider JSON to AggLlmResponse, plus diagnostics. Returning a buffered response to libsy. encode_response AggLlmResponse to provider JSON, plus diagnostics. Returning a buffered answer in the caller's format. translate_response Source provider JSON to target provider JSON. Direct buffered-response conversion. decode_stream_event One parsed provider event to LlmResponseStreamEvent. Retaining the source event alongside neutral chunks. encode_stream_event One LlmResponseStreamEvent to zero or more provider events. Replaying or converting incremental output. finish_stream Stream state to any remaining target events. Closing the target format after the source stream ends.

Buffered encoders return TranslationOutput with the encoded body and TranslationDiagnostic values. Inspect diagnostics from decoding and encoding; the direct translation helpers combine them and annotate source/target formats.

docs.title: Policies
docs.text:
These defaults come from TranslationPolicy::default().

Field and type Default Meaning TranslationPolicy.unknown_field_policy: UnknownFieldPolicy UnknownFieldPolicy::Preserve Keep unknown provider fields where the codec can retain them. Alternatives warn and drop, or reject. TranslationPolicy.lossy_conversion_policy: LossyConversionPolicy LossyConversionPolicy::AllowWithDiagnostics Allow known losses and record warnings. Use LossyConversionPolicy::Reject to fail on known lossy conversions. TranslationPolicy.deterministic_ids: DeterministicIdPolicy DeterministicIdPolicy::GenerateStable, prefix sw Generate stable IDs when needed. The alternative preserves IDs without generation. TranslationPolicy.preservation: PreservationPolicy PreservationPolicy::InMemory Retain original parsed bodies in protocol values for replay. TranslationPolicy.target_capabilities: TargetCapabilities All capability fields unspecified Optionally constrain supported tools, media, reasoning, schema output, and other target features.

Unspecified capabilities are not proof that a model supports a feature. A provider can still reject the encoded request. Known-loss rejection covers the codec's implemented checks, rather than proving semantic equivalence for every possible provider extension.

docs.title: Preservation and edits
docs.text:
An original body takes precedence over reconstructed fields for its own format. The codec looks up a request in PreservationMetadata.requests, or a buffered response in PreservationMetadata.responses.

Policy Behavior Boundary PreservationPolicy::InMemory Keep original JSON in protocol values. Same-format replay works while that preservation data remains available. PreservationPolicy::Embed Also embed preservation metadata in translated JSON. Supports multi-hop round trips when intermediaries retain it; provider metadata limits can prevent use. PreservationPolicy::Disabled Do not use preservation for replay. Encoders reconstruct the body from current protocol fields.

If you edit a decoded request, remove that format's entry from PreservationMetadata.requests or encode with PreservationPolicy::Disabled. This applies to model changes, messages, generation settings, and schema enforcement. Apply the same rule to buffered response edits.

Replay preserves parsed JSON values, not original HTTP bytes, whitespace, or headers. Input cleanup can happen before capture, including removal of Codex internal compaction markers. Request.raw_request is host-owned and is not the codec's replay source. Preserved data can contain the full conversation and other sensitive provider fields.

docs.title: Stream translation
docs.text:
Use a separate StreamTranslationState for each response stream. Feed parsed provider events to decode_stream_event, pass the resulting event to encode_stream_event, and call finish_stream when the source closes. The encoder may emit several target events for one input event.

When the source and target formats match, a preserved event replays its retained JSON. Cross-format encoding uses normalized chunks. After changing a stream event, use replace_normalized() to clear raw data that no longer describes it. The response reference explains what aggregation retains and drops.

docs.title: Conversion limits
docs.text:
Retention and destination support are separate. Anthropic has no distinct developer authority, the OpenAI formats have no standard tool-result error flag, and provider built-in tools or encrypted reasoning may lack equivalents.

Use ProviderExtensions and preservation to retain source data, then inspect diagnostics and the destination model's capabilities. For a custom format, FormatCodec and StreamCodec define the codec contracts; TranslationEngine::with_registries accepts explicit registries.

docs.title: Advisor-Gate Routing
docs.text:
Advisor-gate routing pairs an executor (the model under test, serving every client-visible turn) with a stronger advisor that acts as a quality gate. The executor works the task with its own tools; when it produces a terminal turn — a plan before doing the work, or a claim that the task is complete — the advisor reviews the session transcript and either lets the turn through (APPROVE) or discards it and sends the executor back to work with a concrete plan (REDO). The advisor is judge-only: it reviews turns but never serves one, so clients only ever see executor output.

This differs from the classifier and router strategies: those decide which model serves a turn, while the advisor gate keeps one model serving and spends the stronger model only on verdicts at the moments that decide task success.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Every request routes to the executor. The gate buffers each executor turn, decides whether it needs review, and only then releases it to the client.

A review fires on one of two triggers:

  • no_tool_call (default) — the executor's first turn without tool calls, the natural "I'm done or I have a plan" moment on function-calling agent harnesses. gate_min_tool_results skips early chatty turns: a no-tool-call turn is only reviewed once the conversation carries at least that many tool results.
  • pattern — the first turn whose visible text matches gate_trigger_pattern, for text-protocol harnesses where every turn lacks tool calls and completion is declared with a textual marker instead.

Independently, gate_stall_turns adds a mid-task checkpoint: when a conversation reaches that many assistant turns without ever triggering, the next turn is reviewed once — catching executors that grind without declaring completion.

The advisor receives the serialized transcript (task, actions, results, and the gated turn) under a reviewer contract that demands APPROVE or REDO as the first word of its reply. On APPROVE the buffered turn replays to the client verbatim, preserved provider events included. On REDO the turn is discarded — the client never sees it — and the advisor's plan is appended as user feedback, the executor re-invoked, and its continuation served instead.

%%{init: {"flowchart": {"nodeSpacing": 18, "rankSpacing": 26}}}%%
flowchart LR
    t["executor turn"] --> g{"trigger fires?"}
    g -->|no| r["replay to client"]
    g -->|yes| c["advisor reviews transcript"]
    c -->|APPROVE| r
    c -->|REDO| f["discard turn, inject plan,\nre-invoke executor"]
    f --> r

    classDef box font-family:monospace,fill:none,stroke:#9aa0a6,stroke-width:1px;
    class t,g,r,c,f box;

Reviews draw from a per-session budget of max_reviews. The budget scope is the caller's proxy_x_session_id header when present — benchmark harnesses stamp every request of one evaluation with it, sub-agents included, so the budget means "reviews for this task" even behind a gateway shared by many tasks — then the session id resolved from harness headers (such as x-switchyard-session-id), and one scope per server when neither is present. A failed consult refunds the review budget and counts toward a separate cap of 3. An unparseable verdict also refunds the budget and passes the turn through as APPROVE.

Long sessions are truncated middle-out before the consult: the transcript keeps the task statement at the start and the most recent work at the end, marked ...<middle of the conversation truncated>..., capped at transcript_max_chars. fail_open (default true) lets the buffered executor turn through when the advisor call fails after its client's retries or deadline, and /v1/stats counts the failure under advisor_gate.consult_failures. With fail_open = false the request stops with a server error instead.

Gate behavior is observable at /v1/stats under advisor_gate: verdicts by trigger, consult failures by reason, and REDO-discarded turns with their token counts (the client never saw those turns, so terminal usage accounting alone would miss them).

docs.text:
[targets.executor]
id = "small/model"
llm_client = "provider"

[targets.advisor]
id = "frontier/model"
llm_client = "provider"

[routes.gated]
id = "switchyard/gated"
type = "advisor"
executor_target = "executor"
advisor_target = "advisor"
max_reviews = 3
gate_stall_turns = 30
gate_min_tool_results = 3
Key Default Meaning executor_target required Serves every client-visible turn. advisor_target required Reviews gated turns; never a routing destination. gate_trigger "no_tool_call" What fires a review: no_tool_call or pattern. gate_trigger_pattern unset Regex for the pattern trigger; required by and exclusive to it. max_reviews 1 Review budget per session scope; later triggers re-review until spent. gate_stall_turns 0 (off) Mid-task checkpoint after this many assistant turns. gate_min_tool_results 0 Minimum tool results before a no_tool_call turn is reviewable. advisor_max_tokens 2048 Output cap for each advisor consult. advisor_temperature unset Sampling temperature for consults; omitted when unset. transcript_max_chars 200000 Middle-out cap on the serialized transcript (~50k tokens). fail_open true Failures returned to the core algorithm pass the turn through. The Rust runner stops HTTP client failures regardless of this setting. reviewer_system_prompt built-in Overrides the APPROVE/REDO reviewer contract. redo_feedback_prefix built-in Overrides the prefix injected before a REDO plan.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
The defaults gate once per session at the first terminal turn. On agentic coding harnesses, the configuration that benchmarked best is max_reviews = 3, gate_stall_turns = 30, gate_min_tool_results = 3: skip the early commentary turns, keep a mid-task checkpoint for grinders, and allow a re-review after a REDO.

Expect the gate's value to depend on the executor. On Terminal-Bench 2.1 with a coding agent it lifted a weak executor by 11 points (43.8% → 54.7% ± 0.7, k=3) by catching premature "done" claims and stalls, while on a strong executor it only matched the accuracy of the takeover-style routers — strong executors rarely produce the diligence failures a review can catch. If your executor is already frontier-class, benchmark stage-router routing first; reach for the advisor gate when the executor is markedly weaker than the best model you can call, or when you need a review trail rather than a model swap.

docs.title: Composite Routing
docs.text: Routing algorithms composed together. One sets the configuration of another and hands off, so each algorithm runs where its evidence is strongest. The composition is not restricted to a tree: sequential, conditional, and turn-boundary shapes all fit the same route type.

docs.title: What exists today
docs.text:
One pairing: a classifier selects the stage router's starting policy. An efficient classification selects efficient-first with efficient_first_threshold (default 0.5). A capable classification selects capable-first with capable_first_threshold (default 0.0). Both thresholds are configurable from 0.0 to 1.0. Tool signals can still change the tier during execution. Both algorithms and the relationship between them are fixed, and the configuration below names them directly rather than composing arbitrary algorithms.

Under capable-first, stage.efficient_hold_turns defaults to -1: after switching to efficient, it stays there until session state is cleared. Efficient-first defaults to 0. Set this field explicitly to override either default; 0 disables the hold, and a positive value holds that many subsequent requests.

The classifier can use an LLM judge or a decision model. A decision model is configured through a decision client and target, separately from the capable and efficient completion targets.

The general form, where any algorithm can target another and set its configuration, is the direction rather than the current behaviour. Expect this route's configuration to change as more pairings are added.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
[routes.switchyard]
id = "switchyard"
type = "composite"

[routes.switchyard.classifier]
target = "judge"
base_threshold = 0.5
classify_trigger = "user_turn"

[routes.switchyard.stage]
capable_target = "strong"
efficient_target = "weak"
efficient_first_threshold = 0.5
capable_first_threshold = 0.0

[routes.switchyard.stage.tool_semantics]
observe = ["lookup_customer"]
mutate = ["update_inventory"]
plan = ["create_research_plan"]
new = ["send_message"]

[routes.switchyard.classifier] is required and takes the stage_router classifier fields. classify_trigger sets how often the judge runs: user_turn re-picks the tier whenever the user speaks, new_session picks once and holds it. [routes.switchyard.stage] takes the stage settings, but accepts neither picker nor a second classifier. The outer classifier supplies the default tier. confidence_threshold remains an alias for efficient_first_threshold. Custom tool_semantics remain stage-local and have the same additive behavior as on a standalone stage route.

docs.title: Custom LLM classifier
docs.text:
To select a tier directly with your own prompt, keep the stage block and use:

[routes.switchyard.classifier]
mode = "custom"
target = "judge"
classify_trigger = "user_turn"
max_output_tokens = 64
prompt = 'Choose efficient unless capable offers a concrete advantage for this task. Return JSON with decision.target set to efficient or capable.'
response_schema = '''
{"type":"object","properties":{"decision":{"type":"object","properties":{"target":{"type":"string","enum":["efficient","capable"]}},"required":["target"],"additionalProperties":false}},"required":["decision"],"additionalProperties":false}
'''
policy = { type = "target_selector", selector = "/decision/target" }

The schema is validated locally. The selector names a tier, and the existing stage targets supply its model. Custom classifiers always fall open: a missing or invalid verdict or a client failure retains the previous tier, or uses the configured stage default for a new session. A failed new_session judgment retains that fallback so tool continuations do not call the judge again. fail_open = false is rejected for custom classifiers. Capability thresholds and decision-model settings cannot be combined with mode = "custom".

docs.title: Decision model classifier
docs.text:
Use a decision target as the classifier. Keep the stage block above and replace its LLM classifier settings with:

[decision_clients.decisions]
format = "system_one"
endpoint = "https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions"
api_key_env = "OPENROUTER_API_KEY"
timeout_ms = 5000

[decision_targets.judge]
id = "inception/mercury-decide:free"
decision_client = "decisions"

[routes.switchyard.classifier]
target = "judge"
classify_trigger = "user_turn"

[routes.switchyard.classifier.decision]
cutoff = 0.4
candidates = { a = "strong", b = "weak" }
evidence = { description = "Add task-relevant evidence comparing a and b." }

Both candidates must be completion targets. The judge must be a decision target. See the decision client reference for OpenAI Decisions configuration.

The classifier selects capable when probabilities.advantage exceeds cutoff. Calibrate the cutoff for your tasks and models. Omit LLM-only settings such as base_threshold, threshold_step and prompt when using a decision model. On judge failure, the default is to retain the last classified tier or use efficient for a new session. Set classifier.fail_open = false to return the error.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
The tier is retained per session, so send x-switchyard-session-id and each conversation keeps its own. A client that sends no session ID can set classifier.message_hash_fallback = true, which keys on the first user message instead. Conversations that open with the same text then share a tier.

Rust code that calls Algorithm::run_stream directly can store the tier itself. Pass the stored State to run_stream, save RoutingOutcome.state after each turn, and send no session ID. With a session ID, the router uses its own session state and returns the passed State unchanged. switchyard-server starts each request with an empty State, so server clients still send x-switchyard-session-id.

docs.title: Example use
docs.text: An interactive coding agent in auto-mode. The classifier reads the user turn and picks the tier. The stage router runs the tool execution loop on its own signals until the next user turn.

docs.title: Escalation-Router Routing
docs.text:
Escalation routing starts each conversation on a cheaper weak model. An LLM judge reads how the work is going and latches the session to a strong model when it detects sustained trouble. An optional de-escalation policy can later return the session to the weak model.

Use it for multi-turn agent workloads where a weak model handles routine work but may need rescue after repeated errors, loops, or drift. Unlike plain LLM Classifier Routing, which predicts how difficult a request looks before running it, escalation judges whether the run is actually going well.

docs.title: Configure an escalation route
docs.text:
schema_version = 1

[llm_clients.openrouter]
format = "openai_chat"
base_url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1"
api_key_env = "OPENROUTER_API_KEY"

[targets.judge]
id = "google/gemini-3.5-flash"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[targets.strong]
id = "anthropic/claude-opus-4.7"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[targets.weak]
id = "moonshotai/kimi-k2.6"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[routes.agent]
id = "agent"
type = "llm_classifier"
mode = "escalation"
classifier_target = "judge"
strong_target = "strong"
weak_target = "weak"
prompt = "Judge whether the weak model is stuck. Return the required structured verdict."
escalation = { confirmations = 2, recent_turn_window = 28, window_message_chars = 500 }

classifier_target is the judge. The route's id, agent, is the model name clients send; the judge is not exposed as a client-selectable model.

The route id also reaches the client's own model handling. Agent harnesses such as Codex pick their tool surface, base instructions, and context limits from the model name they are configured with before the request leaves the client, and Switchyard sees the request only afterwards. A route id that matches a client's known model slug runs that client on the model-specific surface; an id that matches none runs it on the client's generic surface. Choose the route id deliberately for the surface you want the efficient tier to work on, and keep it stable across runs you intend to compare, because Switchyard cannot change the client's choice from the server side.

The route-level prompt key replaces the packaged trajectory-judge prompt. It uses the escalation verdict schema rather than the capability verdict schema. Switchyard supplies that schema according to the route's response_format_type: through the structured-output request in the default json_schema mode, or in the prompt in json_object mode. The verdict includes an escalate decision, a bounded failure category, whether the newest turn adds new_evidence, and a short reason. When de-escalation is enabled, Switchyard appends the phase-specific verdict contract to packaged and custom prompts.

docs.title: How the decision works
docs.text:
For each turn on an unlatched session, Switchyard:

  1. Calls the weak target and buffers its reply.
  2. Appends that reply to the transcript and asks the judge to rule on the completed turn. The judge therefore rates work the weak model actually did, not a prediction about work it might do.
  3. Increments a confirmation streak only when an escalate verdict cites fresh evidence for the same failure category as the preceding vote. A different category starts a new streak at one; a decline or stale evidence resets it to zero.
  4. Serves the buffered weak reply when the streak has not yet reached confirmations — so a judged turn that does not escalate costs one weak call plus one judge call, and no strong call.
  5. Discards the buffered weak reply and serves the strong target instead once the streak reaches confirmations. That turn is billed for a weak call, a judge call, and a strong call.

By default, a latched session routes straight to the strong target with no judge call:

%%{init: {"flowchart": {"nodeSpacing": 18, "rankSpacing": 26}}}%%
flowchart LR
    t["turn"] --> p{"streak >= confirmations?"}
    p -->|yes| s["route strong; skip judge"]
    p -->|no| c["call weak, buffer reply"]
    c --> j["judge the completed turn"]
    j -->|decline: streak = 0| w["serve buffered weak reply"]
    j -->|escalate, not yet confirmed| w
    j -->|escalate, confirmed| l["discard weak reply; serve strong"]

    classDef box font-family:monospace,fill:none,stroke:#9aa0a6,stroke-width:1px;
    class t,p,s,c,j,w,l box;

An unparseable verdict serves the buffered weak reply and holds the existing streak. The Rust runner stops the request if an HTTP model call fails after retries. To bound both the weak-model response and the judge response, set timeout_ms on each [llm_clients] entry they use. The deadline applies separately to each call, even when both models share a client. Expiry returns 504 without calling another target or selecting the strong tier for subsequent session turns.

docs.title: Judge model compatibility
docs.text: The trajectory judge uses the same response contract and provider/model compatibility guidance as the LLM classifier judge. See Judge model compatibility.

docs.title: Tuning options
docs.text:
The judge exposes three base settings. Their defaults are the benchmarked configuration, so a bare escalation = {} is a valid, tuned route:

Key Default Meaning confirmations 2 Consecutive fresh-evidence verdicts for the same failure category required before the session latches to strong. Must be at least 1. recent_turn_window 28 Trailing messages shown to the judge on top of the anchors. Must be at least 1. window_message_chars 500 Per-message truncation cap inside that trailing window. Must be at least 50.

Replace the inline escalation value in the example with nested tables to make escalation reversible:

[routes.agent.escalation]
confirmations = 2

[routes.agent.escalation.deescalation]
strong_min_calls = 3
confirmations = 2
strong_max_calls = 6
weak_cooldown_calls = 8
De-escalation key Required Default Meaning strong_min_calls Yes — Strong-tier turns before release is allowed. Must be at least 1. confirmations Yes — Consecutive judge declines required to return to weak. Must be at least 1. strong_max_calls No unset Hard limit on strong-tier turns before forced de-escalation. Must be at least strong_min_calls. weak_cooldown_calls No 0 Weak calls served without judging after a hard-limit return.

With this table present, Switchyard marks judge input as either EFFICIENT_EVALUATION or STRONG_EVALUATION. In the strong phase, escalate: true keeps the strong tier; the router reads only escalate there, so category and new_evidence are reported but do not affect release. An escalate: false verdict can release the next request only after strong_min_calls is reached and the configured confirmation streak is complete. A timeout, error, or unparseable verdict retains the strong tier. Omitting the table preserves the permanent latch and does not add phase markers to judge input.

The strong-phase verdict is judged against the trouble that caused the escalation: the packaged rules release only once the failure that triggered the latch no longer shows in the recent results and the strong tier has verified its fix, and they retain while it is still diagnosing, editing, or has not yet run the confirming check.

When strong_max_calls is set, the request after that many strong-tier turns returns to weak even if the judge has not released it. weak_cooldown_calls then prevents immediate re-escalation and avoids turn-by-turn bouncing.

If the strong target is unavailable during a review, the normal candidate fallback may serve the weak target. Switchyard does not judge that fallback as a strong answer, clears any partial release streak, and retries the strong phase on the next turn.

confirmations is the main cost dial. 1 latches sooner and spends more on the strong tier. 2 or higher requires a session identity, because the streak is retained per session — without one, every turn starts from zero and the route never latches. De-escalation also requires a session identity to retain its phase and confirmation counts. Clients supply it with x-switchyard-session-id.

When stateful escalation receives no session ID, Switchyard logs one warning per route. The request still succeeds, but its temporary state cannot carry into the next request.

Anchor and transcript caps remain fixed. Set the route-level max_output_tokens key to change the judge's reply budget. Any decline or verdict without new evidence resets the streak to zero.

docs.title: Run the route
docs.text:
After installing the Rust server, as described in Local Evaluation, export the provider credential, validate the configuration, and start the binary:

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="your-openrouter-key"  # pragma: allowlist secret
switchyard-server --config routes.toml --dry-run
switchyard-server --config routes.toml \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4000

Send a request using the route ID, supplying a session identity so the streak persists across turns:

curl http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "x-switchyard-session-id: demo-session" \
  -d '{"model":"agent","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hello"}]}'

Invalid settings are rejected when the configuration loads rather than on the first request, so --dry-run catches them.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
Read the standard stats endpoint:

curl -s http://localhost:4000/v1/stats

The snapshot reports per-model calls, token usage, and latency for the strong and weak tiers. Judge calls are recorded in the classifier stats bucket, so their token usage and latency remain visible as routing overhead. Dollar costs are not included. Calculate them separately using the recorded usage and model pricing.

When the server runs with a routing log, successful judge calls also appear in per-session routing stats under the judge's model id, tagged with the classifier tier — so per-session token accounting includes judge overhead alongside the tiers the session was served by.

The server log records each parsed escalation verdict's escalate decision, category, and new_evidence flag. The judge's free-form reason is neither retained nor logged.

docs.title: When not to use escalation routing
docs.text:
• One-shot requests. No trajectory to judge. Use LLM Classifier Routing in capability mode.
  • Traffic without session identity. With confirmations above 1, the route cannot accumulate a streak and never latches.
  • Fixed traffic experiments. Use Random Routing.
  • Per-turn stage optimization. Use Stage-Router Routing when signals should move individual turns in both directions.
  • Latency-critical traffic. An unlatched turn waits for the weak call and then the judge call.

docs.title: LLM Classifier Routing
docs.text:
Task routing uses the LLM classifier's capability mode to judge whether an efficient model can handle the task or a capable model is needed. Configure it with type = "llm_classifier" and mode = "capability".

The same classifier also supports escalation and custom routing across two or more targets.

For a task-level decision-model example with structured instructions, see the Jev routing profile.

docs.title: Configure a classifier route
docs.text:
This example uses the packaged classifier prompt as intended: it estimates whether the weak target can complete the task, and keeps the first routing decision for later requests in the same conversation.

schema_version = 1

[llm_clients.openrouter]
format = "openai_chat"
base_url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1"
api_key_env = "OPENROUTER_API_KEY"

[targets.classifier]
id = "openai/gpt-4o-mini"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[targets.strong]
id = "openai/gpt-4o"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[targets.weak]
id = "z-ai/glm-5.2"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[routes.smart]
id = "smart"
type = "llm_classifier"
mode = "capability"
classifier_target = "classifier"
strong_target = "strong"
weak_target = "weak"
base_threshold = 0.5
threshold_step = 0.1
classify_trigger = "new_session"
message_hash_fallback = true

message_hash_fallback is best-effort: independent sessions with the same first user message share an affinity key. Prefer an explicit x-switchyard-session-id when repeated opening prompts are possible.

The target table names are local references. Their id values are the model identifiers sent to the upstream provider. The route's id, smart, is the model name clients send to Switchyard.

docs.title: How the decision works
docs.text:
The classifier target returns a structured verdict containing:

  • p_solve: the estimated probability that the weak model completes the task.
  • capability_boundary: supported, uncertain, unsupported, or unmatched.
  • primary_rule: the capability-card rule that determines the boundary.
  • crux: the hardest material requirement for whole-task success.

For a usable verdict, Switchyard routes to weak_target when p_solve is greater than or equal to the applicable threshold. Otherwise it routes to strong_target:

  • supported uses base_threshold.
  • uncertain and unmatched use base_threshold + threshold_step.
  • unsupported uses base_threshold + 2 * threshold_step.

An invalid, inconsistent, or unparseable verdict routes to strong_target. Raising either knob sends more traffic to the strong model.

To stop waiting for a judge that accepts the request but never finishes its response, set timeout_ms on the judge's [llm_clients] entry (see the TOML schema); it covers the judge's retries and the complete verdict body. When the deadline expires, the Rust server returns 504 without calling strong_target or weak_target. Other HTTP client failures also stop routing after retries. The deadline applies to every call through that client. Give the judge its own entry if the answering models need a different deadline, even when they use the same provider. Without a deadline, the request can wait indefinitely for the judge.

docs.title: Judge model compatibility
docs.text:
The judge must return complete, schema-valid JSON in normal assistant content. Switchyard does not parse provider-specific reasoning fields such as reasoning_content. If content is empty or unparseable, the route falls back to strong_target even when the judge request returned HTTP 200. With session affinity, that fallback can be reused without another judge call.

Capability and escalation routes use JSON Schema structured output by default. For a provider that supports JSON Object mode but not JSON Schema, set response_format_type = "json_object" on the route. Switchyard then adds the verdict schema to the judge prompt and validates the returned object locally.

When a vLLM-compatible provider supports enable_thinking, configure it on the judge target through extra_body:

[targets.classifier]
extra_body = { chat_template_kwargs = { enable_thinking = false } }

enable_thinking is a provider-specific vLLM option, not a general requirement for reasoning models. Other model/provider pairs may work with reasoning enabled or use a different control. Verify the judge response shape before deployment. If reasoning remains enabled, set max_output_tokens high enough for both the reasoning and final JSON. A truncated verdict has the same fail-open result. See the target-level extra_body reference for the server merge behavior.

docs.title: Tuning options
docs.text: Key Default Meaning base_threshold required Lowest p_solve that routes a supported task to weak_target. Must be between 0 and 1. threshold_step 0.0 Amount added for each boundary step. Must be finite and non-negative, and base_threshold + 2 * threshold_step must not exceed 1. recent_turn_window unset When unset, the judge sees the opening user task and the latest user message when they differ. When set to N, it sees the opening user task and the last N conversation messages after that task. 0 keeps only the opening task. Client system and developer instructions are not shown to the judge. classify_trigger every_request When the judge runs. every_request judges every request, tool continuations included. user_turn judges each new user message and holds that target across the tool calls between. new_session judges once and reuses that target for the session. message_hash_fallback false When session metadata is absent, keys affinity from the first user-message text. Requires classify_trigger = "new_session" or "user_turn". prompt packaged capability prompt Replaces the classifier's system prompt. The packaged verdict schema and routing policy remain active. response_format_type json_schema Structured-output mode for capability and escalation judges. Use json_object for providers without JSON Schema support. max_output_tokens 4096 Maximum completion tokens available to the classifier verdict. Must be at least 1.

docs.title: Override the classifier prompt
docs.text:
Set prompt on the route when the packaged capability rubric does not describe your weak model. Do not copy the response schema into the prompt: Switchyard supplies it according to response_format_type.

[routes.smart]
id = "smart"
type = "llm_classifier"
mode = "capability"
classifier_target = "classifier"
strong_target = "strong"
weak_target = "weak"
base_threshold = 0.5
prompt = """
Estimate whether the weak target can complete the request.
Return exactly one JSON object matching the response schema supplied with the request.
"""

The override changes the instructions only. The judge must still return the packaged crux, primary_rule, capability_boundary, and p_solve fields.

docs.title: Custom multi-target routing
docs.text:
Custom mode accepts an inner JSON Schema and a policy that reads the validated verdict. The policy selects one of the route's model groups, and you name those groups yourself, so a route can choose between as many models as you like.

[routes.smart]
id = "smart"
type = "llm_classifier"
mode = "custom"
default_target = "premium"
prompt = """
Choose the best group for this request.
Return JSON matching the response schema supplied with the request.
"""
response_schema = '''
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "decision": {
      "type": "object",
      "properties": {
        "target": {
          "type": "string",
          "enum": ["fast", "balanced", "reasoning", "premium"]
        }
      },
      "required": ["target"],
      "additionalProperties": false
    }
  },
  "required": ["decision"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
'''

[routes.smart.models]
judge = ["classifier"]
fast = ["fast"]
balanced = ["balanced"]
reasoning = ["reasoning", "premium"]
premium = ["premium"]
any = ["fast", "balanced", "reasoning", "premium"]

[routes.smart.policy]
type = "target_selector"
selector = "/decision/target"

The names in models reference existing target tables. Switchyard passes the schema to the provider in a strict structured-output wrapper and validates the returned JSON again. jsonptr resolves the selector against that verdict. A missing, non-string, or unconfigured label falls back to default_target, and judge is never routable.

A verdict names a group, and the first model in that group serves the turn. Later entries are that group's own fallbacks: if the serving call fails, the client falls through the rest of the chosen group first — reasoning retries on premium above — and then through whatever models.any adds. Every group's targets must also appear in models.any; one that does not is rejected when the configuration loads. models.judge supplies the judge call's own candidates in order and is not a completion destination.

capable and efficient are reserved names. Use them when you want a group to carry the tier meaning the stage and composite routers give it; otherwise any name works.

This separation applies to every classifier mode. Prompts containing the legacy {{RESPONSE_SCHEMA}} placeholder are rejected during configuration validation.

docs.title: Forecast and policy assumptions
docs.text:
The packaged prompt forecasts whole-task success for a generic efficient agent. It produces a probability and capability boundary but does not choose a route. The deterministic policy applies base_threshold and threshold_step after generation.

Without affinity, the runtime judges every request. By default, it sends the opening task and the latest user follow-up when they differ, excluding tool calls, tool results, and reasoning. It keeps ordinary user content from messages that also contain tool results. Set recent_turn_window when intervening conversation context affects the forecast. If a client sends only a follow-up fragment without the opening task, enable affinity or include the task history. Threshold tuning changes routing policy; it cannot recover missing task context.

docs.title: When the judge runs
docs.text:
classify_trigger sets how often the target is re-decided.

every_request, the default, judges every request. In an agentic session that includes every tool continuation, so twenty tool steps means twenty-one classifications of one task, and the target can change between any two of them.

user_turn judges each new user message and holds that target through the tool calls that follow:

[routes.smart]
classify_trigger = "user_turn"

Tool results are the agent continuing work the user already asked for, so they do not re-open the decision. A failed or unusable verdict keeps the current target. When no target has been selected yet, the next request is judged again.

new_session judges once and reuses that target for the rest of the session, including strong_target when it was selected as the fallback for an unusable verdict. There is no warmup period, and later requests skip the judge entirely.

The selection is held in per-session state, so requests without a session identity are judged every time. Clients can send x-switchyard-session-id, or enable message_hash_fallback to key on the first user-message text under new_session.

docs.title: Responses continuations by ID
docs.text:
A Responses API client can continue without resending the conversation history. Switchyard handles state differently depending on the target API:

  • Native Responses targets: The provider stores the conversation. When answer targets use different [llm_clients] entries, Switchyard records response and conversation IDs with the model that served them, but no transcript. Classifier-only clients do not count. When answer targets share one client, no local record is needed. The provider's store value takes precedence over the request value. If it is false, Switchyard skips the response ID but still records the conversation ID.
  • Chat Completions or Anthropic Messages targets: For incoming Responses requests, Switchyard retains request and reply messages in memory under the response ID. It restores that history on a later previous_response_id request. This also applies when answer targets share one client. Request store: false prevents retaining the new response and history, but does not delete earlier records. This path supports previous_response_id, not provider conversation IDs.

A request with a recorded ID returns to the model that served it without a judge call or fallback to another provider. This applies to every classify_trigger and to stage_router and composite routes. Tracking covers buffered replies and completed streams, including answers returned by /v1/decision. Ordinary Chat Completions and Anthropic Messages requests do not create Responses history.

Each route keeps up to 65,536 distinct ID-to-model records per process. This limit counts response and conversation IDs recorded over the process's lifetime, not tokens or simultaneous requests. Records do not expire, and Switchyard does not remove older records to make room. Cross-format records also retain message history, so this ID limit is not a memory limit. Memory use depends on the retained messages as well as the number of IDs.

At capacity, Switchyard logs a warning and returns the reply without retaining new IDs or history. Existing records remain usable, but a later continuation from an unrecorded ID may fail. Conflicting native Responses IDs return HTTP 409 with code response_state_conflict. If streaming headers have already been sent, the stream emits an error instead of changing the HTTP status.

A restart removes all local records and history, and each replica has its own state. Unknown IDs use normal routing and can still fail at the selected provider. Send the full history instead of an ID to avoid relying on local continuation state and to keep dynamic routing across turns.

docs.title: Run the route
docs.text:
After installing the Rust server, export the provider credential, validate the configuration, and start the release binary:

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="your-openrouter-key"  # pragma: allowlist secret
switchyard-server --config routes.toml --dry-run
switchyard-server --config routes.toml \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4000

Send a request using the route ID:

curl http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"smart","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain why the sky appears blue."}]}'

Treat the selected target as model-dependent output, not a fixed test result.

docs.title: Model Selection
docs.text: Switchyard routes each request to one of the models you configure. The models you put in each role change results more than any threshold does. This page says what each role needs, how to check a model before you route to it, which pairs have measured results, and the mistakes we have seen in real runs.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Each strategy names its models by role. The TOML keys differ by route type:

Route type Serves most turns Takes the hard turns Decides auto, stage_router, composite efficient_target capable_target Tool-result signals. composite adds a classifier. plan_execute efficient_target, after the first edit capable_target, while planning The first file edit. llm_classifier (capability, escalation) weak_target strong_target The judge at classifier_target. llm_classifier (custom) Your target names Your target names The judge in models.judge. advisor executor_target advisor_target reviews. It does not serve turns. The gate rules.

A role is not a property of a model. The same model can be the capable tier in one route and the efficient tier in another. See the model pool example.

What each role needs:

  • Capable, strong, or advisor. Your best model on this workload. Every escalation lands here. Routing cannot solve a task this model cannot solve.
  • Efficient, weak, or executor. Serves most turns. It must call the agent's tools correctly, follow the output format, hold the agent's context, and still complete tasks. Judge it by the tasks it completes on your workload, not by its price.
  • Judge or classifier. Returns schema-valid JSON on every call, and does so quickly. See Judge model compatibility.

docs.title: Check the efficient model before you route
docs.text:
Run these checks before you measure routing. Add a passthrough route for the efficient model to the file from Local Evaluation, start the server with --routing-log-file routing.jsonl, and send the checks to that route:

[routes.efficient_only]
id = "efficient-only"
type = "passthrough"
target = "efficient"

docs.title: 1. Tool calling
docs.text:
Send a request with one tool and read the call back:

curl -s http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "efficient-only",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "What is the weather in Paris? Use the tool."}],
    "tools": [{"type": "function", "function": {
      "name": "get_weather",
      "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"city": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["city"]}}}]
  }' | jq '.choices[0].message.tool_calls[0].function.arguments | fromjson'

Pass: the output is a JSON object with a city key. Fail: null, or a fromjson error. Then run your agent against this route on one short task. Models that pass with one tool can produce malformed calls once the agent sends its full tool list. The agent reports those as invalid tool calls, or it repeats the same step.

docs.title: 2. Structured output
docs.text:
Judges, and some agents, need JSON that matches a schema:

curl -s http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "efficient-only",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Is 7 a prime number?"}],
    "response_format": {"type": "json_schema", "json_schema": {"name": "verdict", "strict": true,
      "schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"prime": {"type": "boolean"}},
                 "required": ["prime"], "additionalProperties": false}}}
  }' | jq '.choices[0].message.content | fromjson'

Pass: {"prime": true}. An HTTP 400 means the provider does not offer JSON Schema mode for this model. For a judge, set response_format_type = "json_object" on the llm_classifier route. See Judge model compatibility.

docs.title: 3. Context window
docs.text:
The efficient model must hold the agent's largest prompt. Find that size after a run through the passthrough route:

jq -s 'map(.prompt_tokens) | max' routing.jsonl

Compare it with the context length your provider lists for the model. OpenRouter reports it as context_length in GET https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models. Set the route's context_window to the smaller of the two tiers' limits so clients that read it compact in time. The server does not enforce it. See the route keys.

docs.title: 4. Reasoning
docs.text:
A model that reasons at length on every turn is slow and costly in the efficient role. Read the reasoning share from the log:

jq -c '{model, completion_tokens, reasoning_tokens}' routing.jsonl

Providers that do not report reasoning tokens leave the field at 0. When reasoning tokens dominate on simple turns, set reasoning_effort on the target for openai_chat and openai_responses clients, or use the provider's own control through extra_body. See Reasoning effort.

docs.title: 5. Wire format
docs.text: format on the LLM client must match the endpoint. --dry-run checks the file only. It does not contact the provider. Send one request to the passthrough route and confirm an HTTP 200 with a choices array. The same model can also behave differently on different endpoints. See Pin the provider and endpoint.

docs.title: Measured pairs
docs.text:
See Benchmarks for consolidated Terminal-Bench 2.1 and DeepSWE results, config links, and evaluation settings.

These pairs have results from checked-in profiles or a public report. Each row describes one pair on one workload. The thresholds and results do not transfer to another pair or another workload. The profile headers give the serving stack, agent version, and scoring rule for each run, and absolute results vary by serving stack.

Efficient tier Capable tier Strategy Workload Result Single-model anchors Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, also the judge Claude Opus 4.7 llm_classifier custom, balanced and aggressive tau2-bench telecom, 114 tasks 0.903 ± 0.071 solve rate with 45% of turns on the weak tier. 0.891 ± 0.029 with about 85%. Within noise of the strong tier, per the profile headers Nemotron 3.5 Lightning Claude Opus 4.8, with Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite as judge llm_classifier escalation, confirmations = 2 LangChain Deep Agents suite, 145 tasks, 5 runs (report) 80.0% at $3.00 per run, with 7% of calls on Opus Opus alone 86.0% at $11.45. Nemotron alone 77.7% at $0.72.

What the rows show about model choice:

  • The gap between the two single models sets the room for routing. Compare the fixed-model baselines with the routing results, as in the DeepSWE studies.
  • When the efficient model is close to the capable model, escalation keeps most of the accuracy at a fraction of the cost. On the LangChain suite the two single models were 8 points apart. Routing kept 80 of the 86 points at about a quarter of the cost.
  • The judge's cost counts. In the LangChain runs the judge took 21.2% of spend. Choose a judge that is small and fast, and include it in the cost per run.

Other checked-in configurations:

  • tb-lite-llm-classifier-opus-kimi-gemini.toml (Claude Opus 4.7 strong, Kimi K2.7 code weak, Gemini 3.5 Flash judge) is a smoke test. It has no published result.

docs.title: Counter-examples
docs.text:
These cases came from users' runs. Each describes one pair on one workload.

  • The efficient model was too weak. A first stage-router run scored below the single capable model. The efficient tier failed tasks the capable model solves, and the signals escalated too late to recover them. Check: run the fixed arms first. When the efficient-only arm is far below the capable-only arm, routing has to escalate a large share of turns to close the gap, and the savings shrink.
  • The pair was inverted. On one coding benchmark the model in the efficient tier solved more tasks than the model in the capable tier. Every escalation then cost more and solved less. Check: the inversion check.
  • The tool list broke the efficient model. A 4-billion-parameter local model called tools correctly in a small test and produced malformed calls once the agent sent its full list of 27 tools. Check: tool calling with the agent itself, not only with a one-tool request.
  • Switching cost more than it saved. A pair matched the single capable model's accuracy but cost more. Each switch between models lost the prompt cache, so the next turn paid full price for the whole prompt, and the efficient model kept too little of the traffic to make up for it. Check: cached_tokens in the routing log on the turn after a model change, and cost per run for the routed arm against the fixed arms, not per-token prices.

docs.title: Check for an inverted pair
docs.text:
Symptom: the routed run scores below the efficient-only run, or GET /v1/stats shows most turns on the capable tier while results do not improve.

Detection: run both models alone on the same tasks. Two passthrough routes in one file do this:

[routes.capable_only]
id = "capable-only"
type = "passthrough"
target = "strong"

[routes.efficient_only]
id = "efficient-only"
type = "passthrough"
target = "weak"

Run your agent against each route ID on the same set of tasks, at least 20. Count solved tasks per arm. Read token use per arm from the routing log:

jq -s 'group_by(.route_id) | map({route: .[0].route_id, calls: length,
  prompt_tokens: (map(.prompt_tokens) | add),
  completion_tokens: (map(.completion_tokens) | add)})' routing.jsonl

Multiply the totals by each model's prices to get cost per arm. The pi integration page shows one way to do that.

Fix: if the efficient-only arm solves at least as many tasks as the capable-only arm, swap the two roles, or serve the efficient model alone with passthrough. If both arms solve the same tasks, routing has little to gain on this workload. The room for routing is the set of tasks only the capable model solves.

docs.title: Pin the provider and endpoint
docs.text:
A model ID does not fix how the model is served. Three things move results between runs.

Provider. Through an aggregator, one model ID can be served by several providers with different quantization, context length, and tool-call support. Symptom: the same configuration gives different results on different days, and the routing log's model field does not change. Detection: the aggregator's response metadata or dashboard shows which provider served each call. Fix: pin the provider in the target's extra_body. On OpenRouter, order names the providers to try and allow_fallbacks = false stops it from trying others:

[targets.weak]
id = "qwen/qwen3-35b-a3b"
llm_client = "openrouter"
extra_body = { provider = { order = ["your-provider"], allow_fallbacks = false } }

Use the provider slug from the model's page on OpenRouter.

Endpoint and wire format. The same model can behave differently on openai_chat, openai_responses, and anthropic_messages. One measured case is Claude behind an LLM gateway. On anthropic_messages the thinking level worked and the prompt cache was read. On the two OpenAI formats a thinking level returned HTTP 400, and openai_responses never read the cache. See Claude through an LLM gateway. Record format and base_url with every result.

Streamed token counts on /v1/messages. When a client uses Anthropic Messages and the selected target is on an OpenAI format, the streamed message_start event reports input_tokens: 0. The counts the upstream reports arrive in the final message_delta event. Symptom: the client shows zero prompt tokens, or a context meter that never moves, for turns served by those targets. Detection: compare the client's numbers with prompt_tokens in the routing log, which records the upstream's counts. Fix: read usage from message_delta, or use the routing log and GET /v1/stats for accounting.

docs.title: Reasoning effort
docs.text:
Effort changes a model's results and cost as much as the model choice does. Record it with every result. Three rules apply:

  • On openai_responses the effort field is reasoning.effort. A top-level reasoning_effort key in extra_body does not set it. Use the target's reasoning_effort key instead. It writes reasoning.effort on openai_responses and reasoning_effort on openai_chat, replacing the value the client sent. The DeepSWE profiles above use it to run both tiers at max.

  • reasoning_effort is rejected on anthropic_messages clients. The server does not start:

    target weak reasoning_effort is only supported on openai_chat and openai_responses clients

    For those targets the effort the client sends is passed through in Anthropic's form.

  • One route cannot hold the same model at two efforts. Two targets with the same model ID on one client but different reasoning_effort or extra_body fail to load:

    targets strong and strong_max both name model openai/gpt-4o on llm client openrouter but with different reasoning_effort, extra_body, or omit_body_fields; one target per model id is kept, so give each its own model id or llm client

    Separate routes can use separate llm_clients entries for the same endpoint. See the target keys.

docs.title: Routing Overview
docs.text:
The switchyard-server binary loads a native TOML deployment. Each route's id becomes a model ID available through OpenAI Chat Completions, Anthropic Messages, and OpenAI Responses requests.

Use this page to choose a routing strategy, then open its detailed page for configuration and tuning. Mechanics of Libsy explains the execution model; Switchyard Protocols explains the request and response data.

docs.title: Choose a strategy
docs.text:
Start with Auto. Choose Task or Execution when you want more control over how requests move between an efficient model and a capable one.

Choice Use it when Route type Auto You want Switchyard's recommended preset. auto Task You want an LLM to judge which model can handle the task. llm_classifier Execution You want tool results and agent progress to guide each request. stage_router

Task uses the LLM classifier's capability mode. Its classify_trigger setting controls whether the judge runs for each request, each user turn, or once per session. Execution uses the stage router, which reads tool-result history and can optionally call an LLM judge. The TOML configuration keys are unchanged.

Whichever strategy you choose, the two models you put behind it matter more than any threshold. See Model Selection. To tune cost against quality, follow the tuning loop.

docs.title: What the names mean
docs.text: Name Route type What it does Auto auto The Execution preset with fixed settings. Task llm_classifier, mode = "capability" A judge reads the task before the turn is served and picks the strong or weak model. Execution stage_router Tool results from the last few turns pick the capable or efficient model for each turn. Composite composite A judge picks the starting tier at each user turn. Execution runs the turns in between. Plan/Execute plan_execute The capable model plans. The first file edit hands the session to the efficient model. Escalation llm_classifier, mode = "escalation" The weak model serves until a judge reports the same failure on consecutive turns. Then the session latches to the strong model. Custom llm_classifier, mode = "custom" Your own judge prompt and schema choose among any number of targets. Advisor Gate advisor One executor serves every turn. A stronger advisor reviews its plans and "done" claims. Verification-Gated vgr An efficient model drafts. Verified answers stay on the efficient tier, and everything else goes to the capable model. Random random A fixed traffic split. Fixed passthrough One target, no decision. Sub-agent subagents table A separate policy for delegated sub-agent work on passthrough, stage_router, and composite routes.
