docs.title: When routing will not help
docs.text:
Each strategy page lists the cases it does not fit: stage router and escalation. These cases apply across strategies:

  • Requests carry no session ID. Escalation never latches, at any confirmations. Composite cannot retain the tier. Task with user_turn or new_session judges every request. Plan/Execute needs the first edit to stay in the request history. Execution keeps no capable hold. Send x-switchyard-session-id, or use a strategy that decides from the request alone.
  • Both tiers resolve to the same model, or the efficient model is the stronger one. Routing then only adds cost. Run the inverted-pair check first.
  • Chat-only traffic on Auto or Execution. With no tool results the signals abstain and every turn lands on the efficient tier. Use Task or Composite, which judge the request itself.
  • Responses continuations by ID. A client that sends previous_response_id with new input, and no history, hides the tool calls that Execution and Plan/Execute read. See Responses continuations by ID and the Plan/Execute history requirement.
  • A judge that cannot return schema-valid JSON. Task then sends every request to the strong target, Execution falls back to the picker default, and escalation never latches. When the provider rejects the judge request outright, escalation turns fail with that error instead. Run the structured output check and see Judge model compatibility.
  • A judge on every tool step. Task's default classify_trigger = "every_request" judges every tool continuation. An agent that makes twenty tool calls causes twenty-one judge calls for one task. Use user_turn with a session ID, or Execution, which reads the tool results without a model call. See When the judge runs.
  • Sub-agent traffic without identity. A subagents policy applies only when the harness sends sub-agent identity. Otherwise delegated requests follow the parent route. The server logs a warning for Claude Code versions known to lack child identity; other harnesses give no log line. See Sub-Agent-Aware Routing.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Three starting points. Each names a strategy, a file in this repository to copy, and the one dial to move first.

  1. A coding agent, and cost comes first. Start with auto. When you need to tune, copy the DeepSWE stage profile and move confidence_threshold as described in Tuning confidence_threshold.
  2. Long sessions where the cheap model should run until a judge reports that it is failing. Use escalation. Copy the escalation profile, send a session ID, and move confirmations as described in Tuning options.
  3. One executor you want to keep, with a stronger model as a quality gate. Use the advisor gate. Copy the DeepSWE advisor profile and move max_reviews together with gate_min_tool_results as described in Tuning.

For multi-turn support traffic with few tool results, the tau2 custom-classifier profiles are the measured starting point. Their dial is the judge rubric in prompt.

docs.title: Auto
docs.text:
Auto is a preset, not a separate routing algorithm. An auto route builds a stage router with these settings. It does not compare strategies at runtime.

Setting Value What it does picker efficient_first The efficient tier serves a turn when the tool signals are not confident. confidence_threshold 0.5 How strongly the tool signals must agree before they pick a tier on their own. recent_turn_window 3 How many recent tool results the signals are computed over. capable_hold_turns 2 How many turns stay on the capable tier after an escalation, skipping signal processing and classification. Classifier none No LLM judge is called.

Auto accepts no tuning keys. To change a setting, write the equivalent stage_router route shown in the TOML schema and edit it there. Choose the two models with the model selection guide.

Only the efficient_first picker has published results. The capable_first picker is experimental.

docs.title: When Auto does not route
docs.text:
Auto decides from tool results in the request. In these cases every request goes to one tier:

  • No tool results in the request. Chat-only requests, and the first request of an agent session, carry no tool history. The signals abstain and the efficient tier serves the turn. This is by design. GET /v1/stats counts these turns under algorithm_stats.stage_router.routing_decisions.fall_open. See Verify routing is active.
  • Both tiers name the same target. The server accepts a route whose capable_target and efficient_target are the same target. Every request then goes to that one model, and GET /v1/stats lists a single entry under .models.
  • No session ID on the request. The capable hold is kept per session. A request without a session ID gets fresh state, so a hold set by one request is gone on the next. Requests with a session ID but no agent ID share one hold within that session.

A critical error, a repeated identical failure, or a context-compaction marker in the tool history still sends the turn to the capable tier. See decision sources.

Auto uses the settings of the published stage-router results, with two differences: those runs set recent_turn_window = 5 and added a handoff note. Every published result comes from a coding agent whose requests carry tool results. The model selection guide lists the measured model pairs.

docs.title: Common route shape
docs.text:
A deployment has three layers. LLM clients describe how to reach a provider, targets name models on those clients, and routes decide which target serves a request:

schema_version = 1

[llm_clients.openrouter]
format = "openai_chat"
base_url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1"
api_key_env = "OPENROUTER_API_KEY"

[targets.strong]
id = "openai/gpt-4o"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[targets.weak]
id = "openai/gpt-4o-mini"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[routes.fast]
id = "fast"
type = "passthrough"
target = "weak"

[routes.smart]
id = "smart"
type = "random"
targets = ["strong", "weak"]
weights = [3, 7]

Clients send a route's id (fast or smart) as the request's model ID. The table name in [routes.smart] is local to the file; only id is visible to clients. A single deployment can serve multiple routes on the same host and port.

Credentials stay outside the file: api_key_env names an environment variable that is read at startup. Omit it for an upstream that needs no credential, such as a local model server.

The examples use model IDs from the OpenRouter model catalog. Select IDs available to your account before deploying; catalog availability can change.

docs.title: Direct model routes
docs.text:
A passthrough route registers one target under one model ID with no routing decision:

[routes.fast]
id = "fast"
type = "passthrough"
target = "weak"

Use a routing strategy instead when requests must be split or classified across targets. There is no catalog auto-discovery, so to expose several upstream models, add one passthrough route per model.

docs.title: Self-hosted targets
docs.text:
Any target can point at an OpenAI-compatible model server you operate. For example, start a local vLLM server:

vllm serve ./my-rl-qwen --served-model-name my-rl-qwen --port 8000

Then declare it as its own LLM client and target. The client needs no api_key_env when the server does not require a credential:

[llm_clients.local_vllm]
format = "openai_chat"
base_url = "http://localhost:8000/v1"

[targets.local]
id = "my-rl-qwen"
llm_client = "local_vllm"

[routes.local]
id = "local"
type = "passthrough"
target = "local"

Switchyard does not start or manage the model server; it only sends requests to the configured endpoint.

docs.title: Run a deployment
docs.text:
After installing the Rust server, as described in Local Evaluation, export the provider credential, validate the configuration, and start the binary:

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="your-openrouter-key"  # pragma: allowlist secret
switchyard-server --config routes.toml --dry-run
switchyard-server --config routes.toml \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4000

Send a request using a route ID:

curl http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"smart","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hello"}]}'

For the complete TOML schema and every route option, refer to the TOML Schema.

docs.title: Plan/Execute Routing
docs.text:
Plan/execute routing uses a capable model to inspect and plan a coding task, then switches to an efficient model after the first recognized edit or write tool call. It does not make a classifier call.

schema_version = 1

[llm_clients.provider]
format = "openai_responses"
base_url = "https://example.com/v1"
api_key_env = "OPENAI_API_KEY"

[targets.planner]
id = "provider/capable-model"
llm_client = "provider"

[targets.executor]
id = "provider/efficient-model"
llm_client = "provider"

[routes.plan_execute]
id = "switchyard/plan-execute"
type = "plan_execute"
capable_target = "planner"
efficient_target = "executor"

Read-only inspection stays on the capable target with a planning instruction. The first edit or write routes the full trajectory to the efficient target and latches that choice by session ID. A failed edit still triggers the handoff. Without a session ID, the first mutation must remain in the request history.

docs.title: Session capacity
docs.text:
Each router instance retains up to 4,096 executing identities in memory. Root requests use the session ID. Subagent requests use the session ID and agent ID. Once retained, an identity stays on the efficient target after history compaction until a request marks it with session_final: true or the router restarts.

At capacity, a new identity's handoff returns an error before calling a model. Existing identities keep their execution phase. Mark an existing identity's last request with session_final: true to free its slot, then retry the handoff with the mutation history intact. The server accepts this flag through the x-switchyard-session-final: true header.

A handoff marked final needs no saved slot and can still run at capacity. Requests that are still planning or have no stable identity also use no slots.

docs.title: Responses API history requirement
docs.text:
Plan/execute needs the conversation history to detect edits and hand the task to the executor. Continuing with only previous_response_id or a provider conversation ID and new input is not supported for this handoff.

For example, a function_call_output contains the result and call ID, but not the tool name. Without the earlier write_file call, the router cannot tell that the result belongs to an edit and can stay on the planner.

Send the conversation history in input, including earlier tool calls and their results. Omit previous_response_id and conversation so routing can switch models between turns.

When embedding libsy, your application must supply that history in Request.llm_request.messages before routing. libsy does not fetch it from the provider. A stable session ID remembers a detected handoff, but cannot detect an edit missing from the request history.

docs.title: Optional settings
docs.text:
Key Behavior tool_semantics.mutate Lists custom tools that trigger handoff. planning_prompt Replaces the built-in planning instruction. handoff_prompt Adds an instruction to the handoff request. planner_reasoning_as_text Converts visible planner reasoning summaries to assistant text at handoff.

To make a custom tool trigger handoff:

[routes.plan_execute.tool_semantics]
mutate = ["persist_source_file"]

This uses the same tool matching rules as Stage. The other custom tool categories do not trigger handoff.

Use a stable session ID with handoff processing or history compaction.

docs.title: Prefill routing
docs.text:
Experimental in v0.3.0. Switchyard does not provide or support a router checkpoint, an exporter, or compatible encoder assets. You must obtain or train a compatible checkpoint and obtain its encoder and tokenizer yourself. There is no supported end-to-end checkpoint export and compatibility contract. The steps below describe a research workflow, not a ready-to-run deployment.

Prefill router runs the request through pytorch and transformers to get hidden states. It uses those states as input to a classifier which you have to train. For each model the classifier predicts if it will succeed at the task. This is a variation on using embeddings as input to the classifier.

This makes it different from the other routers in that it both requires running inference (with transformers) and training a classifier for the specific models you intend to use and the specific workload you will send it. This makes it much more complex to deploy than the other routers, but potentially better if you know your workload.

docs.title: How do I use Prefill Router?
docs.text:
1. Define a model pool/ workload for routing
  2. Collect (at a minimum) 3k-5k judged evaluation samples of each model on that workload as training samples
  3. Train router using prefills as inputs + 0/1 labels as outputs (suggested prefill model: Qwen 3.6 35b)
  4. Serve checkpoint through Switchyard

There is some documentation for an older version here: - Collect training data - Train a router

docs.title: Random Routing
docs.text:
Random routing selects one configured target for each request without inspecting the prompt. It supports two or more targets.

Use it for A/B tests, benchmark baselines, and controlled traffic splits. Use a content-aware routing algorithm instead when the request itself should determine the target.

docs.title: Configure a random route
docs.text:
This example sends approximately 30% of requests to a strong model and 70% to a weak model:

schema_version = 1

[llm_clients.openrouter]
format = "openai_chat"
base_url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1"
api_key_env = "OPENROUTER_API_KEY"

[targets.strong]
id = "openai/gpt-4o"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[targets.weak]
id = "openai/gpt-4o-mini"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[routes.ab_test]
id = "ab-test"
type = "random"
targets = ["strong", "weak"]
weights = [3, 7]
seed = 42

The configuration has two layers:

  • [targets.strong] and [targets.weak] define models that Switchyard can call. Their id values are the model identifiers sent to the upstream provider.
  • [routes.ab_test] defines the random route. The table name ab_test is local to the TOML file, while its id, ab-test, is the model name clients send to Switchyard.

docs.title: Control the traffic split
docs.text:
The route's targets list establishes the order:

targets = ["strong", "weak"]

The corresponding weights list assigns a relative weight to each target in that same order:

weights = [3, 7]

The weights do not need to add up to 1; Switchyard treats 3:7 as a 30%/70% split. More generally:

  • Every target name must be unique and refer to a target defined in the same TOML file.
  • weights must contain one non-negative, finite number per target.
  • Omitting weights gives every target equal weight.
  • A weight of 0 disables that target. At least one weight must be greater than 0.
  • seed is optional. Set it to reproduce the same selection sequence for the same request order in tests or benchmarks. Omit it for normal traffic.

Selection is independent for each request, so short runs may not match the configured proportions exactly. Separate turns in the same conversation can therefore use different targets.

docs.title: Run the route
docs.text:
After installing the Rust server, export the provider credential, validate the configuration, and start the release binary:

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="your-openrouter-key"  # pragma: allowlist secret
switchyard-server --config routes.toml --dry-run
switchyard-server --config routes.toml \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 4000

Send a request using the route ID:

curl http://localhost:4000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model":"ab-test","messages":[{"role":"user","content":"hello"}]}'

docs.title: Experimental LiteLLM integration
docs.text: The package's developer guide is the canonical documentation for integrating Switchyard with a Dockerized LiteLLM gateway. Its source-installable client adapts libsy's dictionary contract and demonstrates weighted random routing between model aliases backed by OpenRouter. The guide covers setup, application usage, live end-to-end testing, and a three-task Harbor smoke benchmark.

docs.title: Stage Router
docs.text:
Execution routing uses the stage router to choose a model from tool results and agent progress. Configure it with type = "stage_router".

Stage-router routing sends each request to either a capable model or a typically cheaper efficient one, depending on where the agent is in its run. The goal is to spend the capable model on turns that need exploration or error recovery and let the efficient model carry routine, mechanical work. Choose a required picker for ambiguous turns, tune the split with confidence_threshold, and optionally add an LLM classifier.

Model-call fallback happens after the routing decision. Eligible context-window or availability failures can try the route's other completion target. See Context-Window Handling.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
A tool-using agent's run moves through stages that call for different amounts of model capability. The built-in vocabulary is calibrated for coding agents: it recognizes file observation, mutation, planning, shell activity, and test results.

For each LLM call without an active hold, stage-router estimates the agent's state from the conversation's tool-result history, scoring signals in two directions:

  • RECOVERY → capable: severity (windowed error severity), spinning (deep churn with no reads or writes), and exploring (reading or planning without producing) push toward the capable tier.
  • PROGRESS → efficient: production_intensity (the share of recent recognized operations that are writes or edits) pushes toward the efficient tier with 1.5 times the weight of one signal. Production with no error in the recent window adds 1.2 more signals toward efficient, so clean production resolves a turn to the efficient tier on its own, even when writes are a small share of recent operations.

The axes are corroborative: the signed score is tanh-squashed to a confidence in [0, 1]. One maxed scoring dimension produces about 0.46; corroborating evidence pushes confidence decisively past a 0.5 threshold. Repeated failures, critical-error severity, and context compaction are hard overrides to the capable tier. Active holds bypass signal extraction and scoring. Severity and test results come from tool output that ran something. The contents returned by the built-in read and search tools do not count, unless the tool reports a failure.

confidence_threshold sets how sure that estimate must be before the router acts on the signal alone. Scores inside the ambiguous band go to the optional classifier and then, if it cannot decide, to the picker's default tier. A turn with no tool-result history follows the same fallback path.

The routing decision for one turn:

    heldRoute(["Route to held tier<br/>confidence = 1.0"])

    recovery{"Hard recovery signal?"}

    band{"Outside the<br/>ambiguous band?"}
    classifier{"Usable classifier verdict?"}

    hold -->|Yes| heldRoute

    classDef input fill:#e0f2fe,stroke:#0284c7,color:#0c4a6e,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef process fill:#f8fafc,stroke:#64748b,color:#1e293b,stroke-width:1.5px;
    classDef decision fill:#fef3c7,stroke:#d97706,color:#78350f,stroke-width:2px;

    class start,history input;
    class scorer process;
    class hold,recovery,band,classifier decision;
    class capable capable;
    class heldRoute,signalRoute,classifierRoute,defaultRoute outcome;

Both pickers support capable_hold_turns (default 2) and efficient_hold_turns (default 0 on standalone routes; composite's capable-first policy defaults to -1). A positive value holds that tier for the specified number of requests after a switch, excluding the switch request. Held requests do not restart the counter. A finite capable hold also starts or restarts on a signal-driven capable decision. Active holds return the selected tier at confidence 1.0 before extracting tool signals or scoring. The existing cascade then skips the fallback judge. Passing tests and errors do not end holds early, and held requests receive no handoff notes.

Set either value to 0 to disable that hold, or -1 to pin to that tier after switching into it. The initial selection does not activate a pin. Pins override later signals, including passing tests and critical errors, and skip the fallback judge. If both values are -1, the first tier switch pins its destination. Switches chosen by signals, the fallback judge, or the picker default all count.

Holds use the existing session state and are separate for each agent ID. Supply a stable session ID across requests. A pin ends when that session state is cleared (including session completion, expiry, or a server restart). Values below -1 or above 4294967295 are rejected.

docs.title: Pickers
docs.text:
The picker name says which tier is the default: the tier used when the signals are ambiguous and no classifier verdict is available.

  • efficient_first: efficient is the default; escalate to capable only when the signals (or the classifier) clearly say so. Cost-first.
  • capable_first (experimental): capable is the default; drop to efficient only when the signals (or the classifier) clearly say so. Quality-first.

Both pickers read the same signals; only the default tier differs.

capable_first is experimental

Every published threshold and routing result comes from efficient_first runs. capable_first works and the server accepts it, but it has not been benchmarked, so there are no calibrated thresholds for it and no measured accuracy or cost figures to set expectations against. The server logs a warning at startup when a route selects it. Use efficient_first unless you are running your own calibration. See Reachable scores per picker for what a threshold can and cannot do with each picker.

docs.title: Tuning confidence_threshold
docs.text:
The tool-signal scorer gives each turn a signed score in (-1, 1): negative scores point to the efficient tier, positive scores point to the capable tier, and the absolute value is the confidence. confidence_threshold creates a closed ambiguous band from -threshold to +threshold. Scores outside the band make a signal-based decision; scores inside it go to the optional classifier or fall back to the picker's default tier.

The TOML schema requires you to choose picker explicitly; there is no implicit default.

Set 0.5 explicitly. confidence_threshold is required by the TOML schema; 0.5 is the recommended starting point, derived from many coding benchmarks, and what the example below uses.

docs.title: Reachable scores
docs.text:
The scorer adds a few signals from the recent tool results. Error severity and stalls count toward the capable tier. Writes count toward the efficient tier. Each signal is bounded, so a turn's confidence can only reach a few values. These are the ones that matter when you choose a threshold:

Situation in the recent window Confidence Direction A soft error alone 0.21 Capable A hard error alone, or a stall alone 0.46 Capable Every operation is a write, with a soft error 0.49 Efficient One write among three operations and no error, the smallest clean-production score at the default window 0.69 Efficient A hard error plus a stall 0.76 Capable. The most the signals reach in this direction (0.7616). Every operation is a write and no error 0.87 Efficient. The most the signals reach in this direction (0.8741).

Production turns the stall signals off, so with any production in the window the capable side stays below 0.46. An error in the window removes the clean-production bonus, so with a hard error the efficient side reaches at most 0.24. The unit test scorer_ceilings_match_the_documented_values in crates/libsy/src/algorithms/util/stage.rs pins these values, so a change to the scorer fails CI until this table is updated.

docs.title: Reachable scores per picker
docs.text:
Both pickers use the same score. The picker only sets which direction the signals must prove.

Picker The signals move a turn to Reachable confidence What a threshold means efficient_first Capable (escalation) Up to 0.7616 At 0.5, a hard error alone (0.46) stays in the band, so an escalation needs a second signal, a hard override, or the classifier. Below 0.46, a hard error alone escalates. At 0.77 and above, the signals never escalate; only overrides, capable holds, and the classifier can. capable_first Efficient (offload) Up to 0.8741, and at most 0.49 when an error is in the window At 0.5, clean production offloads (0.69 and up at the default window) and nothing else does. Below 0.49, production with a soft error in the window also offloads. At 0.88 and above, the signals never offload.

Lower the threshold to let the signals decide more turns. Raise it to keep more turns on the picker's default tier. Hard overrides, capable holds, and the classifier do not use the threshold. The server warns at startup that capable_first has no calibrated threshold.

docs.title: What 0.5 means with efficient_first
docs.text:
With picker = "efficient_first", no classifier, and a threshold of 0.5:

  • scores below -0.5 route to efficient from the tool signals;
  • scores from -0.5 through +0.5 are ambiguous and fall back to efficient;
  • scores above +0.5 route to capable from the tool signals.

Hard overrides and capable-hold state can still select capable independently of this score. Lowering the threshold narrows the ambiguous band, so more turns are decided directly by the scorer. Raising it widens the band, so more turns use the picker default (or the classifier, when configured). That movement changes the efficient/capable routing split.

confidence_threshold Behavior Typical use 0.0 Every non-zero score makes a signal-based decision. A neutral score or missing tool history still falls through. Maximize decisions by the tool-signal scorer. 0.5 Scores from -0.5 through +0.5 are ambiguous. Recommended starting point, derived from many coding benchmarks. 1.0 Every ordinary score is ambiguous; hard overrides and capable holds still apply. Classifier-driven when a classifier is configured; picker-driven otherwise.

A route with a 1.0 threshold remains valid without a classifier. In that case, ordinary sub-threshold turns fall back to the picker's default tier; hard overrides and capable-hold behavior still apply.

The signal-vs-classifier split is dataset-dependent. Measure it in production: /v1/stats reports decision counts by source and selected target, plus aggregate scorer metrics. Response headers and structured decision logs explain individual selections.

docs.title: Calibrating the threshold from run data
docs.text:
Use about 10% of your representative tasks. Replay their agent histories through the Stage tool-signal scorer and collect the unthresholded signed score for each ordinary turn. Track hard overrides and capable holds separately because changing the threshold does not affect them. Plot the score distribution, then overlay candidate ambiguous bands.

For efficient_first, count how many turns fall below the band, inside it, and above it. Without a classifier, those regions map to signal-selected efficient, default-efficient, and signal-selected capable decisions. Choose the threshold that gives the routing split you want, then validate it on the same sample before running the full task set.

docs.title: Knob reference
docs.text:
Every key a stage_router route accepts. The handoff_notes and classifier tables are optional. The TOML schema has the full table with required columns.

Key Default Meaning capable_target required Capable tier. efficient_target required Efficient tier. picker required efficient_first or capable_first (experimental). Tier used when the signals are not confident. confidence_threshold required Corroboration a decisive pick needs, 0 to 1. Alias efficient_first_threshold. capable_first_threshold 0.0 Used only after an outer composite classifier selects the capable tier. No effect on a standalone route. recent_turn_window 3 Trailing tool results the signals are computed over. capable_hold_turns 2 Requests kept on capable after switching to it; signal-driven capable decisions also start finite holds. 0 disables; -1 pins after a switch. efficient_hold_turns 0 Requests kept on efficient after switching to it. 0 disables; -1 pins after a switch. tool_semantics.observe [] Domain tool names that count as investigation. tool_semantics.mutate [] Domain tool names that count as production. tool_semantics.plan [] Domain tool names that count as planning. tool_semantics.new [] Domain tool names that count as neutral forward activity. handoff_notes.escalation_note required in the table Note handed to the capable tier when the signals or a hard override escalate. handoff_notes.deescalation_note unset Note handed to the efficient tier whenever the signals select it, with or without a capable turn before. handoff_notes.only_on_wrong_signal_escalation true When true, restricts escalation notes to signal-driven capable decisions. Held turns receive no notes with either setting. classifier.target required in the table Judge target. Not a routing destination. classifier.base_threshold required for LLM judges Lowest p_solve that still routes efficient. classifier.threshold_step 0.0 Added once for uncertain or unmatched verdicts, twice for unsupported. classifier.fail_open true On judge failure, fall open to the picker default instead of failing the request. classifier.decision unset Use a decision model instead of an LLM judge. Excludes the LLM judge keys below. classifier.classify_trigger every_request Only the default is accepted. The judge runs on every ambiguous turn. classifier.message_hash_fallback false Rejected at load. The judge retains no verdict. classifier.recent_turn_window unset Trailing messages the judge sees after the opening task. A different unit from the route's recent_turn_window, which counts tool results. classifier.prompt packaged Replaces the judge prompt. classifier.response_format_type json_schema json_object for providers without JSON Schema. classifier.max_output_tokens 4096 Token budget for the verdict. subagents unset Separate policy for delegated sub-agent work.

classifier.response_schema, classifier.policy, and any classifier.mode other than capability belong to composite routes and are rejected here. classifier.mode = "capability" is accepted and changes nothing.

docs.title: Minimal route
docs.text:
schema_version = 1

[llm_clients.openrouter]
format = "openai_chat"
base_url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1"
api_key_env = "OPENROUTER_API_KEY"

[targets.capable]
id = "openai/gpt-4o"
llm_client = "openrouter"
# system_prompt = "diagnose before you edit"  # optional

[targets.efficient]
id = "openai/gpt-4o-mini"
llm_client = "openrouter"
# system_prompt = "follow the settled plan"  # optional

[routes.stage]
id = "switchyard/stage"
type = "stage_router"
capable_target = "capable"
efficient_target = "efficient"
picker = "efficient_first"
confidence_threshold = 0.5
recent_turn_window = 3          # optional, defaults to 3
capable_hold_turns = 2          # optional, defaults to 2
efficient_hold_turns = 0        # optional; -1 pins after switching to efficient

Save as routes.toml and start the server:

switchyard-server --config routes.toml --port 4000

This is the recommended default: routing on tool signals alone, no classifier.

docs.title: Optional: custom tool semantics
docs.text:
Extend the built-in coding vocabulary when an agent uses domain-specific tool names. Mappings are route-scoped, additive, and matched by exact name without regard to ASCII case:

[routes.stage.tool_semantics]
observe = ["KB_search", "get_customer_by_phone"]
mutate = ["send_payment_request", "update_inventory"]
plan = ["create_research_plan"]
new = ["start_conversation", "send_message_to_user"]

The categories affect existing stage signals:

  • observe counts as investigation, like the built-in read and search tools.
  • mutate counts as production, like the built-in write and edit tools.
  • plan counts as investigation, like the built-in planning tools.
  • new records forward activity that suppresses false spinning and exploring signals, but does not otherwise favor either tier.
  • Unmatched tools remain unknown; there is no unknown configuration key.

Configuration cannot reclassify a built-in tool. Empty names, duplicate names across categories, and unknown category keys are rejected when the route is loaded. Argument-aware wrapper tools, inferred semantics, and learned routing rules are outside this exact-name configuration.

MCP tools match by their bare tool name or by their full name. Claude Code sends an MCP tool as mcp__<server>__<tool>, and Codex sends it with a separate namespace. For both, send_payment_request matches the send_payment_request tool on the billing MCP server, and so does mcp__billing__send_payment_request. A server name that contains __ needs the full name.

docs.title: Optional: handoff notes
docs.text:
Add a [routes.stage.handoff_notes] section to append contextual guidance to a request when tool signals decide its tier. Notes exist only in the forwarded request; they do not accumulate in the caller's conversation. The escalation note accompanies a signal-driven capable decision, and the optional de-escalation note accompanies a signal-driven efficient decision.

[routes.stage.handoff_notes]
escalation_note = "the previous model was stalling; pick up the diagnosis"
# deescalation_note = "..."          # optional
# only_on_wrong_signal_escalation = true  # default; held turns never receive notes

Classifier and picker-default decisions do not add handoff notes.

docs.title: Optional: LLM classifier fallback
docs.text:
The block is optional. Without it, an ambiguous turn goes directly to the picker tier.

To judge ambiguous turns with a model call, add the block. The classifier runs when the scorer has no tool history or produces a score inside the closed ambiguous band:

[targets.stage_judge]
id = "openai/gpt-4o-mini"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[routes.stage.classifier]
target = "stage_judge"     # judge-only; never a completion destination
base_threshold = 0.5       # p_solve floor to route efficient; below this → capable
threshold_step = 0.1       # +0.1 for uncertain/unmatched; +0.2 for unsupported
recent_turn_window = 3     # trailing turns added to the opening task
prompt = "Estimate whether the efficient target can complete this request."
response_format_type = "json_object"  # optional; default is "json_schema"

prompt replaces the packaged capability-classifier prompt. In the default json_schema mode, Switchyard sends the verdict schema through the structured-output request. Set response_format_type = "json_object" for providers that only support JSON Object mode; Switchyard then adds the schema to the judge prompt and validates the returned object locally. The verdict schema and routing thresholds remain unchanged.

The nested stage table in Composite Routing does not accept a classifier block. Its outer classifier supplies the tier used when the stage signals are ambiguous.

Give the classifier its own LLM client or quota bucket where possible. Sharing one provider bucket with the efficient tier adds a request per classified turn and can cause sustained 429s at scale.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
When a model serves the request, the response identifies it with this routing header:

Header Content x-model-router-selected-model The model ID that served the response, including any model-call fallback.

docs.title: Decision sources
docs.text:
The router labels each resolved turn with a decision_source. /v1/stats counts turns by it under algorithm_stats.stage_router.routing_decisions, and the stage router override log line carries it for overrides:

Source When override A repeated failure, critical-error severity, or context-compaction marker forced the capable tier. Structured logs set override_reason to repeated_failure, critical_error, or compaction. capable_hold A hold or pin kept this turn on capable. Any switch to capable can start it; signal-driven capable decisions also start finite holds. efficient_hold A configured hold or pin kept this turn on the efficient tier. dimensions The signed score fell outside the ambiguous band and selected a tier. ambiguous The signed score stayed inside the band. This label never reaches /v1/stats or the logs: the turn continues to the classifier or the picker default, and that later source is recorded. llm-classifier The signals were ambiguous and the classifier returned a usable verdict. fall_open The signal scorer abstained and the classifier was absent or could not decide, so the picker default was used.

docs.title: When not to use stage-router
docs.text:
• Single-model deployments. Use a passthrough route instead.
  • Probabilistic A/B splits. Use Random Routing (type = "random"). The stage-router's signals are wasted on a fixed traffic ratio.
  • No tool-result history. Stage-router needs meaningful tool-call traffic to populate its signals. For pure chat-completion workloads, the signal scorer abstains; the optional classifier decides, or the request uses the picker default when no classifier is configured.

docs.title: Sub-Agent-Aware Routing
docs.text:
Sub-agent-aware routing leaves parent-agent traffic with its configured routing algorithm while routing delegated sub-agent work separately. It is available on passthrough, stage_router, and composite routes through the optional subagents table.

schema_version = 1

[llm_clients.openrouter]
format = "openai_chat"
base_url = "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1"
api_key_env = "OPENROUTER_API_KEY"

[targets.parent]
id = "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[targets.classifier]
id = "openai/gpt-4.1-mini"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[targets.worker]
id = "openai/gpt-5.4-mini"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[targets.reviewer]
id = "anthropic/claude-opus-5"
llm_client = "openrouter"

[routes.agent]
id = "agent"
type = "passthrough"
target = "parent"
context_window = 400000
tool_calling = true
reasoning = true

[routes.agent.subagents]
type = "llm_classifier"
mode = "custom"
models = { judge = ["classifier"], capable = ["reviewer"], efficient = ["worker"], any = ["worker", "reviewer"] }
default_target = "efficient"
classify_trigger = "new_session"
max_output_tokens = 64
prompt = """
Select exactly one target for the delegated task.

- Select "capable" for code review, critique, auditing, or correctness analysis.
- Select "efficient" for implementation, research, explanation, and other delegated work.

Return only JSON matching the response schema.
"""
response_schema = '''
{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "target": {"type": "string", "enum": ["capable", "efficient"]}
  },
  "required": ["target"],
  "additionalProperties": false
}
'''
policy = { type = "target_selector", selector = "/target" }

Set OPENROUTER_API_KEY, save the configuration as routes.toml, and validate it before starting the server:

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY="sk-or-v1-..."  # pragma: allowlist secret
switchyard-server --config routes.toml --dry-run
switchyard-server --config routes.toml --port 4000

The subagents table has its own model groups, separate from the parent route's. A category name in the sub-agent table always means the sub-agent's own models, even when the parent route uses that category too, and the parent never falls back onto a model only the sub-agents were given.

The parent always uses parent. For a delegated request, the classifier sees the prompt supplied by the parent and selects one configured target. With classify_trigger = "new_session", Switchyard reuses that decision for later requests from the same session + agent identity. Use every_request to classify each delegated request. user_turn is not supported for sub-agent routing. Harness-maintenance requests continue through the parent route.

To use Stage Router for parent traffic, replace the [routes.agent] table in the example with the following. The nested [routes.agent.subagents] classifier is unchanged.

[routes.agent]
id = "agent"
type = "stage_router"
capable_target = "reviewer"
efficient_target = "worker"
picker = "efficient_first"
confidence_threshold = 0.7
context_window = 400000
tool_calling = true
reasoning = true

The parent stage route may also declare [routes.agent.tool_semantics] to map domain-specific tools; delegated sub-agent policy configuration is unaffected.

Clients must still request the route ID (agent above). An explicit model name that is not registered as a route is rejected before sub-agent classification. message_hash_fallback is not supported for sub-agent routing because affinity requires harness-provided child identity.

Claude Code sends child identity (x-claude-code-agent-id) starting with version 2.1.139. Older builds send only the session id, so Switchyard cannot tell a sub-agent request from the parent's and routes it through the parent route. When a route with a subagents table sees an older Claude Code, Switchyard logs one warning that a harness upgrade may be required. Upgrade Claude Code to 2.1.139 or later.

To send every delegated sub-agent request to one fixed target without calling a classifier, replace the subagents table above with:

[routes.agent.subagents]
type = "passthrough"
target = "worker"

docs.title: Verification-Gated Routing
docs.text:
Verification-Gated Routing (VGR) generates a candidate on an efficient tier. For a final answer, it gathers bounded evidence about that exact candidate and serves it only when the policy allows it. All other final-answer outcomes use the capable tier. Missing context, unavailable verifiers, malformed verdicts, and expired decision deadlines fail closed to the capable tier for final answers.

Tool-calling turns continue on the efficient tier unless the turn judge provides evidence to escalate. An unavailable or inconclusive turn judge leaves the tool turn on the efficient tier. An efficient endpoint failure triggers capable fallback.

docs.title: Configure a route
docs.text:
Declare efficient, capable, and optional verifier targets using the normal deployment schema, then reference their target names:

[routes.assistant]
id = "assistant"
type = "vgr"
efficient_target = "efficient"
capable_target = "capable"
judge_target = "efficient"
capable_judge_target = "capable"
mode = "shadow"
deadline_seconds = 30
task_typing = true
breaker_threshold = 5
breaker_cooldown_seconds = 30
confirmed_recovery_min_clean_tail = 1

judge_target defaults to efficient_target. capable_judge_target is optional. The efficient and capable targets must resolve to distinct model IDs. Set the route's context_window to advertise a configured limit through /v1/models; this works with any supported local service and takes precedence over discovery.

Context discovery is disabled by default. For llama.cpp, set context_discovery = "llama_cpp" on the efficient target's [llm_clients.<name>] entry and leave the route's context_window unset. Switchyard then reads the service's /props response and advertises a positive context capacity when available. Missing or invalid properties leave the capacity unknown; routing continues normally. Discovery does not configure the service or load a model.

See the local-server example for an active llama.cpp configuration and commented Ollama/vLLM alternatives. For Ollama and vLLM, set context_window to match the running service; automatic discovery for those servers is not implemented.

The judge reads its verdicts from the first token's logprobs, so its scored calls turn thinking off: they send reasoning_effort = "none" and chat_template_kwargs = {"enable_thinking": false} on openai_chat targets. Candidates and the judge's deliberation keep the target's own setting. If a Chat backend explicitly rejects this template switch with HTTP 400 or 422, the SDK retries once without it, within the same deadline. Other request fields and the configured transient retry budget are preserved. The target's omit_body_fields can omit the switch from the first call. Custom hosts must handle provider compatibility themselves.

The server caches the model catalog, including unavailable discovery results, for one minute. Discovery probes run concurrently with a two-second total budget per refresh. Completed discoveries are retained when that budget expires.

confirmed_recovery_min_clean_tail, when set, lets an agentic run that recovered from tool errors commit on the efficient tier once that many trailing tool results are clean and the capable judge confirms the evidence.

docs.title: Agentic handoff
docs.text:
These settings are off by default:

agentic_handoff = true
efficient_turn_budget_seconds = 600

agentic_handoff tells the capable tier when it takes over tool-using work that the efficient tier previously served. The notice can include the efficient tier's unchecked final message. It is sent at most once per user turn, and only after new efficient work has been served since the previous handoff. The handoff preserves the conversation's existing messages and content. efficient_turn_budget_seconds escalates a user turn once the efficient tier has spent that much wall-clock time on it.

Optional experimental compaction condenses history from the efficient tier into a cached digest when handing off. Enable it on the VGR route:

[routes.assistant]
agentic_handoff = true
compact_handoff = true

compact_handoff defaults to false and requires agentic_handoff = true. Omitting it or setting it to false preserves the full history. Later requests reuse a digest only when their original history prefix matches; a new user turn clears it. An x-initiator: agent message keeps the digest, while x-initiator: user clears it.

The digest is lossy: user updates and tool output are clipped. Non-text tool results become [non-text content]; non-text user updates, including images, are omitted without a marker. Cache savings and task-success effects have not been measured in a matched evaluation.

The notice covers the current request and asks the capable tier to preserve earlier work, inspect its effects, and repeat or undo steps only when needed.

Escalations release when a new user turn is decided on the efficient tier. Set latch_escalation = true to retain the capable tier across later user turns instead. Shadow mode always releases the hold at the next user turn. All configured VGR durations must be positive.

docs.title: Execution limits
docs.text: bounded_efficient defaults to true. Set bounded_efficient = false on the VGR route to disable its decision deadline and efficient_turn_budget_seconds. Candidate generation, task typing, and verification then wait for completion. Client and upstream HTTP timeouts still apply. Configure those timeouts in the harness and Switchyard client for long-running decisions. Configured durations must remain positive even when these VGR limits are disabled.

docs.title: Hermes auxiliary routing
docs.text:
The local-server example exposes switchyard/only-efficient through the existing passthrough router. Hermes can use it for titles and approval checks, independently of the conversation's VGR route. Configure Hermes against the same Switchyard server:

auxiliary:
  title_generation:
    provider: custom
    model: switchyard/only-efficient
    base_url: http://localhost:4000/v1
  approval:
    provider: custom
    model: switchyard/only-efficient
    base_url: http://localhost:4000/v1
    extra_body:
      reasoning_effort: none
      chat_template_kwargs:
        enable_thinking: false

Use the approval thinking controls only with endpoints that support them. Adjust auxiliary timeouts for endpoint queueing and allow concurrent requests on the efficient server when titles must run alongside the conversation.

docs.title: Hermes session headers
docs.text:
Use a Hermes build that supports both provider options below. The session header must stay the same throughout a conversation; each conversation needs its own ID.

model:
  default: assistant
  provider: custom
  base_url: http://localhost:4000/v1
providers:
  switchyard:
    api: http://localhost:4000/v1
    session_affinity_header: x-switchyard-session-id
    initiator_header: true

x-initiator: user releases the turn hold for a person's new request or steer. x-initiator: agent keeps the hold through tool calls, recovery nudges, and automatic continuations. Retries retain the original call's tag. Without a recognized tag, Switchyard uses the message shape to identify a user turn. x-session-id is also accepted as a session-header alias.

docs.title: Served-answer reporting
docs.text:
VGR opts into served-answer reporting through Algorithm::tracks_answers. The SDK summarizes answers only for opted-in algorithms with a session ID; other routers keep their responses and streams unchanged. Custom algorithms and classifiers default to no tracking. Stateful FallThrough routes opt in when a classifier requests reports.

Custom libsy hosts can check tracks_answers() and report AnswerSummary::of(&response) through Algorithm::observe_answer for aggregate responses. For streams, report final_reply = false when serving begins and report the final summary before forwarding the terminal chunk. Use the request's session ID; requests without one retain the existing behavior.

Without a recognized x-initiator header, reported incomplete answers and immediate recovery nudges retain the turn hold and budget. A reply to a complete final answer releases them after a two-second quiet period. Explicit user/agent headers take precedence. Hosts that omit reporting retain message-shape detection.

docs.title: Verification and capable-tier outages
docs.text:
Policy version 1.2 allows the default verification branch to accept a clean efficient attempt when the capable judge approves both the evidence and the answer. A negative or unavailable evidence verdict skips the answer check.

Typed factual answers are verified on the answer itself, including later user turns without tool work. A readout of at least 0.9 can serve the efficient answer; lower scores require capable-tier verification. Scored verdicts require yes and no together to hold at least half the first token's probability.

Coding without tool history can serve the efficient attempt with a clean readout of at least 0.6, or a readout of at least 0.2 plus capable-judge affirmation. Other final-answer branches can use a separate scored verdict after efficient deliberation.

In active mode, an unavailable capable tier can fall back to an unverified efficient answer. That call receives the original request without the capable handoff note. Fallback is disabled by the kill switch, an open efficient circuit breaker, or an image request the efficient tier cannot serve.

docs.title: Serving modes
docs.text:
• off skips candidate generation and serves the capable tier. This is the default.
  • shadow computes a decision but serves the capable tier. It continues evaluating subsequent steps until VGR escalates, then holds the capable tier for the rest of the user turn. A new user turn resumes evaluation, including when latch_escalation = true.
  • evaluate serves the policy decision for isolated evaluation.
  • active serves the policy decision in production and requires active_approval = "prospective-validation-and-canary-approved".

VGR buffers an efficient candidate before releasing it. A streamed candidate that is licensed is replayed as a stream; a rejected candidate is not sent to the client.

x-model-router-selected-model on each response names the tier that served it.

docs.title: Tuning
docs.text:
Routing has two outcomes you can measure: how many tasks the agent completes, and what a run costs. Tuning is the loop below. Every step links the page that explains it, names what it produces, and says what it costs to run.

Start where your goal is:

Your goal Start at Lower cost at the same quality Step 1, then step 4 for the baseline numbers Add a cheaper model safely Step 2 Routing is on, and results got worse Step 5

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
1. Verify routing is active. Follow Verify routing is active. Produces: the selected-model header from two requests and a /v1/stats capture. Costs: two requests, no agent run.

  2. Choose and check the models. Run the five checks on the efficient model, then the inverted-pair check. Produces: a pass or fail per check, and solved tasks plus cost for each fixed arm. Costs: single requests for most checks, one short agent run for the tool-calling check, and one agent run per arm on at least 20 tasks.

  3. Start from a measured profile. Pick the closest row in Measured pairs and copy its profile from benchmark/routing-profiles/. The strategy comparison says which route type fits your traffic. Produces: a route file that passes switchyard-server --config routes.toml --dry-run. Costs: none.

  4. Run the routed arm against the fixed arms. Use the same tasks, agent, and provider for all three arms. The benchmark guide shows the harness the checked-in results used, and the Benchmarks page lists the published results with their configs. Produces: solved tasks and cost per run for each arm. Costs: k runs per arm. The plan/execute and advisor profiles use three runs and report the mean with the sample standard deviation, as in the plan/execute profile header. The stage profile records a single run. A single run cannot separate a small change from noise.

  5. Read the decision mix. For stage routes, read decision sources from /v1/stats. For escalation routes, read the observability section. For advisor routes, /v1/stats reports verdicts and consult failures under advisor_gate. Start the server with --routing-log-file to keep one record per model call: the served call, and each judge call under the judge's model ID. Filter by model before adding up usage. Produces: the routing_decisions capture and the routing log. Costs: none beyond the runs in step 4.

  6. Move one dial. Change one setting, then repeat step 4.

    Strategy First dial Guidance Execution, Auto confidence_threshold Tuning confidence_threshold and Calibrating the threshold from run data Task base_threshold, then classify_trigger Tuning options and When the judge runs Escalation confirmations Tuning options Advisor Gate max_reviews with gate_min_tool_results Tuning Composite efficient_first_threshold and capable_first_threshold What exists today

    Produces: a before-and-after table with the arm results from step 4. Costs: k runs per setting you try.

  7. Record the result. Write down what you ran, in the form the profile headers use:

    • the Switchyard commit;
    • each model with its provider, wire format, and reasoning effort;
    • the agent and its version;
    • the benchmark, the task count, and k;
    • the result band next to the fixed arms;
    • the cost per run.

    The plan/execute profile header records all of these. Produces: the header. Costs: none.

  8. Recalibrate on change. A new model version, provider, wire format, reasoning effort, agent version, or workload moves the operating point, and the thresholds do not carry over. See Pin the provider and endpoint. Return to step 4 with the recorded header as your baseline. Produces: a new header next to the old one. Costs: the runs of step 4.
